newsitem.title: UK: Marine arms dump not harming environment, Britain.
newsitem.headline: Marine arms dump not harming environment, Britain.

text.p: British government scientists have found that more than a million tonnes of explosive and chemical weapons dumped into the Irish Sea after World War Two have not caused ecological harm.

Announcing the results of a year-long inquiry, Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth said on Thursday: "There is no evidence of munitions having had an adverse effect on the marine environment, or the living resources that it supports."
The announcement was a relief to gas and electricity industries which have run cables and pipelines through the Beaufort's Dyke area of the Irish Sea where the arms were jettisoned.
Forsyth said in a written answer to a parliamentary question that the survey had found no evidence of chemical warfare agents such as phosgene and mustard gas.
But he said low to high densities of dumped munitions were found in the area crossed by a submarine gas pipeline between Galloway in Scotland and Northern Ireland.
There were also munitions at certain points along a proposed route for submarine electricity cables linking Scotland and Northern Ireland.
Beaufort's Dyke, an area of deep sea six miles off Scotland's west coast, was used after the war as a dumping ground for unwanted British military material.
